content_metadata.description: A video demonstrating how to create a simple dichotomous key for identifying a set of organisms.

qAndA.answer: The first feature is whether the organism has legs.
qAndA.question: What is the first physical feature used to separate the organisms in the video?
What organism is identified if it has no legs and no eyes?

qAndA.answer: The features are whether the adult has wings and whether it is covered in feathers.
qAndA.question: What two features are used to separate organisms with more than two legs?

qAndA.answer: The purpose is to allow people to identify organisms even if they don't know what they are.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of a dichotomous key?

qAndA.answer: The narrator mentions that it might not work well if other organisms are added because they could confuse the identification process.
qAndA.question: What potential issue does the narrator mention about the created dichotomous key?

activities.description: The narrator explains the purpose of a dichotomous key and introduces the task.
The narrator identifies a physical feature to separate the organisms.
The narrator organizes the organisms based on leg presence.
The narrator further divides organisms without legs based on eye presence.
The narrator identifies a physical feature to separate organisms with legs.
The narrator further divides organisms based on the number of legs and other features.
The narrator concludes the video and mentions part two.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Welcome to making a dichotomous key part one where we will make the flow diagram,
which is needed to make the final dichotomous diagram, which will be in part two.
Here are some almost random organisms, including my son, arranged in alphabetical order.
Our job is to arrange these in a way that a total stranger who doesn't know what any of them are
can identify them. That is the purpose of a dichotomous key. We need to think of a physical feature
that will neatly and clearly separate these organisms into smaller groups.
Something that applies all the time, something that is not subjective or is unsubjective as is possible.
I am going to choose does it have legs? Clear, easy to understand.
And then I'm going to organize these organisms to two groups. At this point it doesn't really matter.
The things without legs and the things that do have legs.
Just two piles not too important right now where they are. We can add in descriptors in this case
this side will say no, this side will say yes. Looking at the organisms with no legs,
I now have to find another physical feature that I can clearly and easily use to separate these.
In this case does it have eyes? Add two lines and we have the first side done.
Now looking at the organisms on the other side, we notice that two of them walk around on two
legs, two of them walk around on more than two legs. So this is the physical feature that I will
use to separate these organisms. We can quickly move these around to be in a group with two
legs and more than two legs. And finally we have defined physical features to separate this group
and this group which I have done as follows. And here we have our completed dichotomous key.
No legs, no eyes, it's a carrot. No legs eyes, it's a snake, et cetera for all the organisms.
This will work fine for these organisms. It probably will not work if other organisms are
added because they will confuse the issue. But if we know our organisms, it works well.
In part two, I'll show you how to convert this into the dichotomous key that we all tend to use
when we're in the field.
